# Last Time Recap

## Conditional Probability

> **Conditional Probability.** Given two events $A$ and $B$ the probability of $A$
happening given that $B$ has happened is denoted by $p(A\mid B)$ and computed by:
$$p(A\mid B)=\frac{p(A\cap B)}{p(B)}.$$

Also, we discussed the following:

> **Total Probability Theorem.** Given an event $A$ and a partition of the sample space
$\Omega$ into pairwise disjoint events $B_1,B_2,\ldots,B_n$, then it holds that:
$$P(A)=\sum_{k=1}^nP(A\cap B_k).$$

So, given the above, we can also write:

$$P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)P(B),$$

given the definition of *conditional probability*. So, the total probability 
theorem can also be stated as:

$$P(A)=\sum_{k=1}^nP(A\mid B_k)P(B_k).$$
So, we can also distinguish whether two events are independent or not. Recall
that two events are independent exactly when:

$$P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B).$$
So, using conditional probabilities:

$$P(A\mid B)P(B)=P(A)P(B).$$
So, in case $P(B)>0$ we also get:

$$P(A\mid B)=P(A),$$
i.e., knowing what is the outcome of $B$ does not affect the probability of $A$.

## Bayes Theorem

> **Bayes Theorem.** Given two events $A,B$ in a sample space, we have:
$$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B\mid A)P(A)+P(B\mid A')P(A')}$$

Evidently, the above theorem boils down to applying the definition of conditional
probability on the enumerator and the Total Probability Theorem on the denominator.
Also, the same holds for more than two events.

A popular scene from the 2008 [21 movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21_(2008_film))
describes the following problem:

> You have three closed doors in front of you $A,B,C$, two of which contain a goat and 
one of which contains a super-car. You are asked first to pick one of the three doors.
After you make your choice, and one of the two goat-doors has been opened,
you are suddenly given the chance to change your choice. What do you do?

Before we make any decisions and computations, lets write an R script to simulate
this:

```{r}
# First, simulate without changing door.
N <- 1000
hits <- 0
for (i in 1:N) {
  # Randomly select which door contains the car.
  car_door <- sample(1:3, 1)
  # Randomly pick one of the three doors.
  player_choice <- sample(1:3, 1)
  if (player_choice == car_door) {
    hits <- hits + 1
  }
}
prob_no_change <- hits / N
print(paste("Win probability with no door change: ", prob_no_change))

# Then, simulate the change of door.
hits <- 0
```
